video_title: Aydin Senkut: Chasing Demand, Not Hype, at Felicis
gist: Felicis founder Aydin Senkut explains his 20-year playbook of chasing demand over hype, backing foundational infrastructure layers (Superbase, Shopify, Adyen) and now capital-intensive 'trillion-dollar markets' like robotics, AI infrastructure and defense. He details sizing robotics off 190M low-skill jobs, contrarian high-margin inference bets amid debt-funded Neoclouds, the 1-2%-of-market-cap acquisition rule, and why ~$1B early-stage funds beat mega funds.

insights.claim: Felicis underwrites early-stage deals only where it can plausibly see at least 100x revenue growth from the entry point, reasoning that if demand is right, revenue follows, and valuation follows revenue.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: A simple screen for venture/growth exposure: demand-justified 100x revenue path, not current valuation momentum.
insights.quote: We like to chase demand. So is there enough demand to justify at least 100x revenue growth or beyond?

insights.claim: Felicis invested in Superbase at the 2021 valuation peak; the business has grown almost 3,000x since, but it took two to three years for the market valuation to reflect the steady, accelerating fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Valuation lags fundamentals in private markets; flat marks on fast-growing companies can be buying opportunities.
insights.quote: the company's business performance has grown like almost 3,000 X since we invested

insights.claim: Senkut argues investors often confuse hype with demand, and that if underlying business growth is strong and accelerating, market valuation eventually catches up regardless of interim stagnation.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Track underlying revenue/usage rather than round valuations when judging private holdings.

insights.claim: At each new investment into a company with existing traction, Felicis treats it as re-underwriting and asks whether growth will accelerate from there, not merely continue.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Later-stage entry is only alpha if you have a non-consensus view on growth acceleration.

insights.claim: Felicis backed Exa, a search-infrastructure company used by AI models and AI companies, despite strong existing traction, on the view it could grow five to 10 times faster because search is shifting away from consumers going to Google.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: AI-agent search infrastructure is a growth category replacing consumer search behavior; watch for second-order impact on Google search.
insights.quote: the non-consensus view is whether that growth can not only continue, but continue at a much sharper rate

insights.claim: Senkut cites Anthropic's growth as an example of a company that surprised skeptics by continuing and accelerating growth at a scale people thought made acceleration unlikely.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Scale-based skepticism about frontier AI lab growth has repeatedly been wrong.

insights.claim: Virtually all of Felicis's fund-maker companies over 20 years have been foundational infrastructure layers: Shopify (commerce), Adyen (payments), Credit Karma (credit score), SendGrid and web/code security, and AI foundational companies like Runway.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Favor picks-and-shovels infrastructure exposure in each tech wave over application-layer bets.
insights.quote: virtually all of our major fund maker companies have been foundational layer infra companies

insights.claim: Felicis did not back vibe-coding/citizen-developer apps Lovable or Replit, which compete fiercely, yet still benefits because virtually all of them use Superbase as the underlying database.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: When the application layer is a knife fight, own the shared infrastructure that all competitors depend on.
insights.quote: we didn't really have to make one of those bets. We still won

insights.claim: Superbase conviction rested on database companies historically being among the most valuable in tech (Oracle, Snowflake), and on citizen developers growing 10 to 100x plus AI agents that all need an underlying database.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Agentic and citizen-developer growth expands demand for databases/backend infrastructure beyond traditional developer counts.

insights.claim: Felicis plays each wave several ways — anchor model company, data supply, manufacturing/parts, and possibly sovereign champions — so that whoever wins the application race, the firm wins.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Portfolio construction lesson: diversify across a theme's value chain to add resilience.

insights.claim: Senkut says the most important raw material for AI is data, and Felicis holds a number of data companies that also consume heavy data-center resources, benefiting from AI beyond model makers.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Derivative AI beneficiaries (data suppliers) can outgrow model companies with less competition.

insights.claim: Mercor, which supplies data to improve AI models, is probably the fastest-growing company ever in Felicis's portfolio.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: AI training-data vendors are among the fastest-scaling businesses of the cycle; expect analogs in robotics data.
insights.quote: Probably the fastest growing company ever in our portfolio.

insights.claim: Senkut sizes the robotics opportunity off roughly 190 million low-skilled jobs in the US, Western Europe and Japan at $20-25k per year; capturing just 0.2% of that would be about $10 billion in revenue.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Even tiny labor-substitution share implies multi-billion revenue for leading robotics companies.
insights.quote: 0.2% of that market would equal to 10 billion in revenues

insights.claim: Senkut believes the new wave of robotics will be as big as a ChatGPT moment or bigger, and that 24/7 reliable robots would expand the market beyond current labor substitution, analogous to how smartphones outgrew Nokia-era expectations.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Robotics TAM estimates anchored on today's labor market likely understate the opportunity.
insights.quote: this new wave of robotics I feel is going to be as big of a chat GPT moment if not bigger

insights.claim: Felicis's anchor robotics bet is Skild AI ("skill.ai"), founded by two Carnegie Mellon professors and former Facebook VPs who are among the most cited in robotics, pioneering synthetic data and reinforcement learning and hiring talent from Tesla — framed as Felicis's OpenAI/Anthropic equivalent in robotics.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Signals where top early-stage capital sees the robotics foundation-model leader.
insights.quote: this is kind of the equivalent of our OpenAI or Entropic bet in robotics

insights.claim: Felicis just signed a term sheet in a US company making robotics parts such as actuators, because if robotics takes off many of these parts are not made in the US, and is hunting robotics-data companies too.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Robotics component supply chain (actuators) and onshoring is an emerging investable bottleneck.

insights.claim: Robotics is capital intensive — models must be built and then scaled across robot types and deployments — but Senkut argues vast demand justifies the capital need.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Expect large, repeated funding rounds in robotics; dilution risk is offset only by demand scale.

insights.claim: Senkut frames the current era as 'trillion dollar markets with billion dollar contracts': in robotics, AI infrastructure, chips and defense, companies reach $1B revenue faster but with heavy customer concentration and years of upfront capex.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Underwrite hard-tech venture for concentration risk and longer pre-revenue capex, but bigger and faster scale.
insights.quote: I like to call it trillion dollar markets with billion dollar uh contracts.

insights.claim: Felicis has shifted reserve strategy for capital-intensive companies, assuming more than one round of investment rather than the single-round software playbook.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Hard-tech venture funds need deeper reserves; check fund reserve ratios accordingly.

insights.claim: Because AI lets anyone build and customize software cheaply, Senkut says the bar to custom software has collapsed, driving big changes in SaaS and forcing investors to ask where value persists.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Bearish signal for undifferentiated SaaS; favor fundamental software layers and capital-intensive moats.
insights.quote: where do you invest in a world where creating software is no longer really that difficult?

insights.claim: Senkut has become more positive on capital-intensive tech than capital-light software, seeing equal or stronger upside in companies solving harder physical-world problems like energy, defense and global resilience.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Venture capital is rotating toward hard tech; defense and energy are now mainstream venture themes.
insights.quote: Defense is not going to go away. The conflicts are here to stay.

insights.claim: Senkut expects sovereignty to matter in energy, AI and possibly robotics, with each continent wanting its own national champion for national-security reasons rather than accepting US or European leaders.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Sovereign-champion demand creates room for regional winners outside the US.

insights.claim: As an ex-Google investor, Senkut avoided ad tech and marketing companies, believing Google and Facebook's ad networks and billion-user bar make it extremely hard for new consumer/ad players to scale.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Incumbent ad-network moats remain a reason to avoid ad-tech startups.

insights.claim: Most AI inference companies chase the same five or six big customers, who use their market power to crush supplier margins.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Concentrated hyperscaler/AI-lab customers compress inference-provider margins; check customer concentration.
insights.quote: they're not going to give you great margin because they know the kind of power they hold

insights.claim: Many inference and Neocloud companies are building infrastructure on debt at roughly 10% higher interest rates, so margins and cost structure matter heavily.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Debt-financed GPU clouds are vulnerable to margin squeezes and capex swings at their big customers.
insights.quote: they're basically building their infrastructure on debt

insights.claim: Felicis backed a less popular inference company that aggregates long-tail demand with order-of-magnitude better margins, so it is not exposed if Google changes capex or Anthropic has a bad year.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Long-tail-customer infrastructure providers are less exposed to hyperscaler capex cycles than those serving top labs.

insights.claim: Senkut calls today's abundance of venture capital 'almost like a tax' that inflates valuations and reduces ownership, while capital concentrates in the same few companies, leaving whole sectors and geographies underfunded.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Opportunity exists in overlooked sectors/geos; the crowded names carry diluted returns.
insights.quote: it's abundant capital out there, but it is not shared equally across all the companies

insights.claim: Valuations of great companies now jump 10x between rounds instead of 2x, creating intense pressure to invest earlier.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Early-stage entry matters more; later-round step-ups compress future multiples.
insights.quote: valuations jumping 10x instead of 2x between the rounds

insights.claim: Felicis runs about 50 companies per fund versus 25, barbelling obvious consensus winners with non-obvious demand-driven bets because returns require being right and non-consensus.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Concentrated consensus portfolios risk diluted returns; diversified non-consensus exposure is the edge claim.
insights.quote: it's not just enough to be right, you also have to be right and not consensus

insights.claim: Senkut sees minimum viable fund scale at roughly half a billion to a billion dollars; beyond multi-billion mega-fund sizes, managers end up fighting the public index for basis points rather than 3-7x multiples.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: LP takeaway: sub-$1B early-stage funds have a better shot at 3-7x than $5-15B platforms.
insights.quote: you're essentially kind of fighting the public index

insights.claim: Felicis's fund is close to a billion dollars yet 91% of investments are seed and Series A; its first fund was $41 million.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Felicis remains an early-stage manager despite fund growth.

insights.claim: Felicis plans special reserves only for the top three or four companies going 'wildly right' (0.1% companies), treats led deals as at least two-round investments, and says equal reserves across the portfolio don't produce outperformance.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Follow-on concentration into breakouts is a key determinant of venture fund returns.

insights.claim: Senkut's rule of thumb: acquirers almost always pay about 1-2% of their market cap for an acquisition, so targeting categories with trillion-dollar potential acquirers provides a downside exit.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Size the M&A downside by acquirer market caps; trillion-dollar buyers support multi-billion exits.
insights.quote: the acquisition price is always around 1 to 2% of their market cap

insights.claim: In today's IPO market, Senkut says companies need roughly $1-10 billion of revenue scale to go public, so Felicis now seeks companies reaching that scale extremely fast.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: The IPO bar is very high; expect continued private-market holding periods and secondaries.
insights.quote: if you don't have like a revenue scale of 1 to 10 billion, it doesn't even matter

insights.claim: Felicis dedicates 10-20% of its time to engineering exits via secondaries, partial sales for niche companies, and salvage sales, recently recovering roughly 40-50 cents on the dollar for a Texas company that had only one acquirer.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Active exit management and secondaries are increasingly central to venture DPI.

insights.claim: Felicis's long-running founder survey shows trust and speed/level of conviction consistently rank as the top two reasons founders choose a VC, and Felicis pledges never to vote against founders.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: VC competitive edge is now trust and conviction speed; investors now pitch founders, not vice versa.

insights.claim: Senkut tells founders 'don't show me the numbers, show me the growth formula', advising them to delay raises until a step-function lever (distribution deal, self-serve launch) is engineered, since premature raises may not get a second shot.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Durable, engineered growth matters more than headline growth rates when evaluating startups.
insights.quote: don't show me the numbers, show me the growth formula

insights.claim: Felicis benchmarks portfolio companies against peers; 3x growth can rank only about 58th percentile in its current vintage.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Top-quartile growth bars in the current venture vintage are well above 3x annual.

insights.claim: Senkut argues talent is universal and outsiders with a chip on their shoulder are hungrier, citing Shopify in Ottawa, Canva (Canvas) in Sydney, Rovio in Finland, Tines in Ireland, a UK chip company and a Berlin AI company.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Non-Bay Area founders can be underpriced due to consensus geographic bias.
insights.quote: we're looking for people that have a chip on their shoulder

insights.claim: Felicis tries to pre-decide the market question in advance through research, so investment decisions focus only on founder and company, enabling generalists to compete with specialists.
insights.speaker: Aydin Senkut
insights.so_what: Thesis-led preparation is how generalist funds keep pace with vertical specialists.
